title: North and West Africa
hookLine: the Maliki school is followed from Morocco to Nigeria, often praying with hands at the sides

lines: A ROW OF WORSHIPERS IN FEZ.
SOME HANDS FOLDED, SOME AT THE SIDES.
cards: A row of worshipers stands shoulder to shoulder in a mosque in Fez, or Dakar, or Kano. The imam says Allahu akbar and the prayer begins. Look along the row at their hands.

Some are folded over the chest or the stomach. Others hang straight down, loose at the sides, the whole way through the standing. A visitor from Istanbul or Lahore might wonder if something was forgotten.
Nothing was. Those loose hands are a quiet signature of Malik's school, carried a long way from Medina.

teach.h: WEST FROM MEDINA, ACROSS THE SAHARA.
teach.b: The Maliki school traveled west from Medina, along the North African coast and across the Sahara.
Today it's followed in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya, in Mauritania, and through West Africa, in Senegal, Mali and northern Nigeria, among other places.

Scholars carried it: teachers in Kairouan in Tunisia, students in Spain, and later the scholars of Timbuktu, with their manuscript libraries. Back on day 110 you met different hands in one prayer. Here's the Maliki side.
The posture is called sadl, letting the arms hang. In the Mudawwana, an early Maliki book recording Malik's answers, he's reported to have disliked folding the hands in the obligatory prayer.
Maliki scholars give reasons: it was the practice they received in Medina, and it guards against leaning or showing off. Then the honest complication.
Malik's own Muwatta records a report that people were told to place the right hand over the left in prayer. So some Malikis fold their hands, and they too point to Malik.
Both postures are found in Maliki mosques, sometimes in the same row. The other Sunni schools fold their hands, in slightly different places, and Shia Muslims pray with their arms at their sides too.

teach.h: ONE PRAYER, WHATEVER THE HANDS DO.
teach.b: And the prayer behind the imam is one prayer, whatever the hands are doing.

how: Across North and West Africa, Maliki Muslims often pray with their arms at their sides (sadl), while some fold their hands; both are found in Maliki mosques.

games.q: you're visiting a mosque in Dakar, and the man beside you prays with his arms hanging loose. what's going on?
o: he's new and doesn't know how to pray.
he's following a Maliki posture with its own reasons.
it's a local custom with no basis in the schools.
games.why: sadl, letting the arms hang, is reported from Malik in the Mudawwana and is found across Maliki lands.

practice: Stand if you can, or sit tall, and let your arms hang loose at your sides; feel the weight in your fingers and breathe.

Then fold your hands in front of you and feel how different that is, closed and gathered, before letting them fall again and staying there. If you pray, you can remember Muslims standing this way in a row somewhere right now.

carryVoice: Your line: hands at the sides. Each posture is a way someone received. Peace, until tomorrow.
